summary:
Beyond the Celestial Scrap (BTCS) is a free, browser-based pixel-art game and interactive archive for children aged 6-10, developed by the PARADOXX team. It also includes the Orbit Archive experience. Players start in a spinning Milky Way, zoom in on the Solar System, pick a planet, and tap the small missions orbiting it. Each mission is a character, like the dog Laika. Each tap opens a short story about what that mission left behind in space. No image files are used: all spacecraft, characters, and planets are generated in code with pixel drawing, noise algorithms, and dithering. The site works on desktop and mobile, supports keyboard navigation and screen readers, and offers a reduced-motion option.

Contribution to the challenge: For the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” theme, every story gives a voice to a piece of discarded or abandoned space equipment. The content is compiled from NASA’s NSSDCA records and the NASA History Office. Each entry links to its sources, so parents and teachers can verify the facts.

Why it matters: Space debris is a growing risk to the satellites we rely on every day, yet it is hard to explain with charts. BTCS turns the issue into memorable stories, making the problem visible to the children who may one day help keep the sky clean.
details:
Function and How It Works

BTCS (Beyond The Celestial Scrap) is a browser-based pixel-art game and interactive archive that teaches children aged 6-10 about space debris through storytelling. The user moves through a four-stage process:

  • Galaxy: In the slowly rotating Milky Way, a yellow marker labeled “you are here” appears. Tapping it zooms in to the Solar System.
  • Solar System: The user picks one of the planets moving along its orbit. When the cursor hovers over a planet, the planet slows down, which makes it easy for children to “catch” it.
  • Planet orbit: Missions that circle the planet like small satellites (a dog, a monkey, a small robot) are presented as characters.
  • Story: Tapping a character opens that mission’s story. For example, Laika’s spacecraft Sputnik 2 kept circling the Earth for months after the mission ended, and re-entered the atmosphere and burned up in 1958. Instead of dry historical facts, the child sees what a mission leaves behind in the sky.

Every entry ends with a source link.

Benefits

  • Making an abstract subject concrete: Space debris feels distant to children because it is usually associated with statistics and equations. Storytelling and play make the subject memorable.
  • Accessible to everyone: It requires no installation, works on desktop and mobile devices, can be used with a keyboard, includes screen reader descriptions for visuals, and offers a reduced-motion option.
  • Reliability: All the data used comes from NASA and ESA. Parents and teachers can therefore verify the accuracy and authenticity of the information presented.
  • Giving visibility to abandoned equipment: In line with the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” theme, it keeps the stories of left-behind spacecraft alive.

Intended Impact

The project aims to help children see space as “a neighborhood that needs care.” The children who play the game today may be tomorrow’s engineers and may help keep the sky clean. Our team’s message can be summed up in two sentences: it is possible to leave fewer objects behind and to remove the largest objects from space; a problem cannot be solved unless it is seen, so we made the invisible problem visible with pixels.

Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

BTCS is a single-file website that runs in the browser and requires no installation. The interface and interactions were built with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks or external libraries. All drawings are rendered with HTML5 Canvas, and sounds and music are generated in real time through the Web Audio API. The project contains no image or sound files.

No separate drawing program was used for the pixel art. Spacecraft, dogs, monkeys, and astronauts were drawn pixel by pixel in code, using color maps built from character strings and small drawing functions (point, rectangle, circle, line). Figures were multiplied using mirror symmetry and color variants. Planets are generated with a value noise / fBm algorithm, and the light-shadow transitions are converted into a four-tone pixel look using Bayer matrix dithering.

Fonts are served through Google Fonts (Press Start 2P, Pixelify Sans, VT323). The “Space Guide” chat section uses the Google AI Studio (Gemini) API and the NASA Image and Video Library API.

Git, GitHub, and Vercel were used for version control, hosting, and testing; the application was tested in Google Chrome and Opera GX. There is no special hardware requirement; a modern Windows computer and mobile test devices were used during development and testing.

Creativity

  • “Every mission is a character”: Instead of presenting NASA’s abstract, numerical data directly, the data is conveyed through characters like Laika, building an emotional connection.
  • Zero image files: All pixel art and planets are generated with code. This approach produced an engaging result and achieved the intended effect.
  • Three nested scales: The user moves between the galaxy, the Solar System, and the planetary orbit by zooming in.
  • Interaction designed for children: Movement that slows on hover creates a “catching” feeling and makes the game easier to use.
  • Detective metaphor: The scientist is the light and the child is the reader of the story; both ask the same question: “What’s out there?”

Factors the Team Considered

  • Target audience: The audience is children aged 6-10, so learning is delivered through storytelling rather than charts and statistics.
  • Accessibility: The application works on any device. Keyboard, screen reader, and motion-sensitivity support make it easy to access from all devices.
  • Accuracy: The site’s data is based on information obtained from NASA and ESA. A source list appears beneath every piece of information used.
  • Scientific foundation: The game’s narrative, satellites, characters, and collision logic are based on real classifications.
  • Balance: The difficulty level of the site was tested with children in the 6-10 target age group and adjusted for them, so learning happens through fun.
  • Theme fit: Instead of equipment left on the Moon and Mars, the focus is on the traces left behind by missions that remain in orbit.
